items.text: Oil prices have pulled back from highs, with WTI and Brent down ~2% from late July, following a temporary Iran truce that eased energy prices in June. However, the resumption of Middle East hostilities has driven WTI back to $88–$90/barrel, pushing national gasoline prices up 39% since end-February. For credit investors, energy volatility remains a key input for consumer spending and transports refinancing risk.

July ISM Mfg beat expectations at 55.6, with the strongest output acceleration since Nov 2021 and employment returning to expansion (52.8) for the first time since Jan 2025. Yet the Fed held rates steady at 3.5–3.75% with three dissenting votes for a hike, signaling some divide on labor momentum. Watch August payrolls closely—recent softness masks divergence between manufacturing and broader labor market.

June PCE fell 0.1% MoM to 3.7% YoY (down from 4.1% in May), with core PCE at 3.3% YoY, both down from May's readings. However, RBC warns June relief may be temporary, with PPI at 5.5% YoY and core PCE at 3.4% through May. Energy shock re-acceleration and services pricing (PMI Prices at 71.1% in July Mfg) pose upside risk to near-term inflation momentum.

ECB deposit rate remains at 2.25% as of early August 2026, while Fed funds are at 3.75%. US ISM Services at 54% in June (down 0.5 pts) indicates still-resilient but cooling services expansion. Curve has steepened to +45 bps (10y-2y), while CCC OAS jumped 15 bps to 1,028 and HY OAS tightened to 278. Policy holds, but credit spreads signal caution on tail risks.

Manufacturing PMI at 55.6 beat consensus of 54.0, yet China's manufacturing PMI fell to 49.2 in July from 50.3, slipping below 50 and indicating contraction. IG OAS tightened to 78 (-3 bps), but CCC deterioration and curve steepness suggest credit investors should be selective; fallen angels and China-exposed credits face headwinds.

US economy continued expansion for the 21st month in row through July manufacturing, and services expansion remains resilient amid stable consumer spending with modest GDP growth near 2% for 2026. But China's growth momentum has stalled, with PMI in outright contraction and domestic demand weak despite AI-driven exports. Late-cycle US resilience masks global bifurcation.

University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment rose to 54.4 in July prelim (beat 51.0 exp), highest since February, supported by easing gas prices. Yet personal saving rate slipped to 2.7% in June, nearly a four-year low, as spending outpaces income. Services and new orders softening in June (55.4 and 55.1 from 57.7 and 57.3) hint at demand ceiling; housing starts rebounded but existing home sales slid.

themeCards.title: China growth stall amid demand shock
themeCards.statusLine: China manufacturing PMI fell to 49.2 in July from 50.3, ending a four-month growth streak and signaling contraction amid weaker new orders and persistent domestic demand challenges.
themeCards.relevance: Special-situations credit exposure to China-listed corporates, onshore bonds, and Chinese issuers of USD debt faces refinancing pressure if Beijing policy remains cautious and domestic growth stalls further.

themeCards.title: Middle East geopolitical energy shock risk
themeCards.statusLine: The resumption of hostilities in the Middle East has driven oil prices sharply higher, with WTI crude fluctuating around $88–$90 per barrel. Shipping disruptions and sanctions risk remain live.
themeCards.relevance: Energy sector credit already stressed; CRE and consumer discretionary remain vulnerable to sustained oil>$90. Shipping, logistics, and auto-related refinancings at risk if oil shock persists.

themeCards.title: US savings rate collapse and consumer fragility
themeCards.statusLine: Personal saving rate slipped to 2.7% in June, a nearly four-year low, as consumers spend in excess of income. Sentiment bump may mask underlying household balance-sheet strain.
themeCards.relevance: Credit quality deterioration in consumer finance, auto ABS, and credit-card backed securities; covenant weakness could accelerate in a downturn. Watch for stress in subprime auto and CLTV 95+ mortgages.

themeCards.title: Services PMI cooling and demand growth ceiling
themeCards.statusLine: Services Business Activity Index fell 2.3 points to 55.4 and New Orders Index dropped 2.2 points to 55.1 in June ISM, signaling resilience but slowing breadth and momentum in core growth sectors.
themeCards.relevance: Soft landing narrative at risk if services orders continue to decelerate; impacts hotel, restaurant, travel-related credit and professional services issuer refinancing windows.

themeCards.title: Credit spread divergence — IG tightening vs CCC blowout
themeCards.statusLine: IG OAS tightened to 78 bps while CCC OAS widened to 1,028 bps; curve steepness (+45 bps 10y-2y) alongside HY OAS tightening to 278 creates cross-asset mispricing and tail risk.
themeCards.relevance: Market pricing assumes stable Fed and no refinance shock, but CCC deterioration suggests high-yield investors are underpricing distress likelihood in 2027–28 maturities. Selective opportunities in fallen angels and refinancing walls.

themeCards.title: Fed rate path clarity lost amid manufacturing surprise
themeCards.statusLine: ISM Manufacturing beat consensus at 55.6, strongest reading since May 2022, yet three Fed officials dissented for a hike, signaling divided guidance. July data strength may slow September cut expectations.
themeCards.relevance: Refinancing waves in 2H26–2027 are now pricing less easing than June expectations; floating-rate credit and CLOs exposed to higher-for-longer; non-bank financials face NIM compression risk.

regime.label: Late-cycle bifurcated
regime.detail: US factory resilience masks services cooling & consumer savings collapse; China contraction signals global demand risk; spreads tight but CCC blowout flags tail risk; Fed on pause with divided guidance.
